S1_incident_reporting.quote: Manufacturers must report any thermal incident involving fire, smoke, thermal runaway, injury, or property damage to the relevant regulator within 24 hours of learning of it, with an initial account of known facts. Affected customers must be notified within 48 hours when the incident indicates a potential safety risk to their unit or household. Suspected incidents must be logged and investigated; uncertainty about cause does not defer the initial report.

S2_thermal_testing.quote: A model with a failure rate above 5% must undergo a documented risk assessment and corrective-action plan with regulator oversight; exceeding 5% alone does not automatically prohibit sale. Buyers and current owners must be able to obtain results for the model they own or are considering purchasing; these results are provided directly to those customers and are not required to be published to the general public.

S3_remote_shutoff.quote: All new home battery models must include remote emergency shut-off capability that can be activated by the manufacturer or an authorized emergency responder to address an imminent safety risk. Units already installed when this standard is adopted must be brought into compliance within 6 years, where technically feasible. Manufacturers must document infeasibility and provide regulators an alternative risk-mitigation plan and schedule.

S4_fire_suppression.quote: All new home battery units must include built-in fire suppression beginning 36 months after adoption of this standard. Regulators may approve an equivalent built-in mitigation technology where evidence demonstrates comparable protection against fire propagation and risk to occupants and neighbours.

S5_customer_disclosure.quote: When any model exceeds 8 thermal incidents per 100,000 installed units of that model in a year, the regulator must promptly review the evidence and require appropriate interim protections. Within 30 days, the regulator must document its determination, including the risk assessment and whether effective corrective measures can adequately address the risk. The regulator must order a recall when it determines that a material safety risk cannot be adequately addressed by less disruptive corrective measures; exceeding the threshold alone does not automatically require a recall.

document.section_notes: The final S2 keeps the 5% failure rate as a trigger for documented risk assessment and corrective action with no sales stop, and lets buyers and owners see per-model results without public disclosure, which protects Northwind's Hearth 10. The final S5 keeps the 8-per-100,000 per-model threshold as a trigger for prompt review and interim protections but makes recall discretionary under a 'less disruptive measures' test, which protects Halcyon's Ember 8 at 9.9. S1 (24-hour reporting) is the strictest section and applies to both companies' unreported incidents.
